pos: n. (a secret, furtive manner of movement or action)
etymology: From Old English stelan, to steal, the same root behind the verb steal; stealth originally named the furtive manner of a thief's movement before broadening to any secret, shame-driven withdrawal.
biblical_def:
And the people gat them by stealth that day into the city, as people being ashamed steal away when they flee in battle.

David's army has just won a decisive victory over Absalom's rebellion, yet the king's own public, excessive grief over his rebel son's death so overshadows the victory that the returning soldiers slip into the city by stealth, as though they had been routed rather than victorious. The text's own simile is pointed: they moved as people being ashamed steal away when they flee in battle, borrowing the furtive posture of defeat to describe men who had actually won. Joab's blunt rebuke to David in the verses following names the danger plainly: a king's misplaced priorities, honoring a rebel son above the loyal men who risked their lives for him, can turn a real victory into something that feels, even to the victors, like shame requiring concealment. Stealth here is not sin in itself; it is a diagnostic symptom, the visible shape disordered leadership and misplaced grief can press onto an entire army's bearing, turning rightful honor into something hidden.

webster_full: STEAL, v.t./v.i. To take without right or leave, and secretly; to move or withdraw secretly.
STEALTH, n. A secret, furtive manner of acting; clandestine procedure.

corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that a leader's disordered priorities can turn rightful honor into something that feels like shame, distorting even a genuine victory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word remains in ordinary, unaltered use.

The pattern it illustrates recurs whenever leaders, in families, churches, or nations, let misplaced sympathy for the guilty eclipse due honor for the faithful. David's grief for Absalom was not wrong in itself, but its excess pressed his loyal soldiers into stealth, a quiet lesson that godly leadership must guard against letting private grief overshadow due public honor.

pos: n. (one who carries the military standard or ensign at the head of an army)
etymology: From standard, the banner or ensign of an army, + bearer, one who carries; the standardbearer's post was the most visible and most dangerous in the ranks, since the standard's fall signaled the army's collapse.
biblical_def:
And shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body: and they shall be as when a standardbearer fainteth.

Isaiah's oracle against Assyria pictures the LORD consuming that empire's glory, its forest and fruitful field, body and soul together, and then reaches for a single, vivid military image to capture the totality of the coming collapse: they shall be as when a standardbearer fainteth. The standardbearer held the most exposed and most consequential position in ancient warfare, the rallying point every soldier's eye depended on; when he fell, the whole formation's morale and order collapsed with him, since there was no longer a visible point to rally around. Assyria's glory, for all its apparent might, is compared not to a defeated army still fighting but to a single fainting standardbearer, a swift, total, almost anticlimactic collapse after such terrifying strength. The image humbles every proud power the way the surrounding chapters humble Assyria specifically: what looks unshakeable from the ground is, before the LORD who consumes it, no sturdier than one fainting man holding a pole.

webster_full: STANDARD, n. A flag or ensign borne at the head of an army or regiment.
STANDARDBEARER, n. The officer or soldier who carries the standard, the rallying point of the ranks.

The humbling the image performs remains perennially needed: every generation tends to regard its own dominant powers as permanent, much as Assyria's contemporaries regarded Assyria. Isaiah's image insists that no power stands beyond the LORD's reach to consume it as swiftly as a single fainting man.

pos: n. (a woman who practices sorcery; one who deals in forbidden, occult arts)
etymology: From sorcerer, through Old French sorcier, from Latin sors, a lot or fate consulted by divination, + the feminine -ess; sorcery sought knowledge or power through forbidden consultation with fate or spirits rather than through the LORD.
biblical_def:
But draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the whore.

Isaiah 57 turns from comforting the righteous dead to a scathing indictment of Judah's idolatrous establishment, summoning them forward under three compounding epithets: sons of the sorceress, seed of the adulterer and the whore. The sorceress names the occult, forbidden practices Mosaic law repeatedly condemned (Exodus 22:18; Leviticus 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:10-12) as a direct rival to trusting the LORD alone for knowledge of the future and protection from harm; adultery and whoredom are the prophets' standing figures for covenant unfaithfulness, chasing after other gods as a wife chasing after other lovers. Isaiah stacks the images because sorcery and spiritual adultery are, at root, the same sin viewed from two angles: both seek from a false source what only the LORD rightfully gives, whether guidance for the future or covenant security and blessing. The chapter goes on to detail the lengths of this apostasy, idols set up on every high hill, children sacrificed in valleys, journeys to foreign kings for help, all tracing back to the same root the opening verse names: trust misplaced in sorcery and adultery rather than the LORD who alone deserves it.

webster_full: SORCERY, n. The practice of magic arts; enchantment by the assistance of evil spirits, or the agency of demons.

Isaiah 57:3 and the Mosaic prohibitions behind it draw a hard line precisely where modern spirituality erases one: seeking guidance, power, or security from sorcery, however repackaged, is covenant unfaithfulness, the same root sin as adultery against the LORD who alone is to be trusted and consulted. The dictionary names the modern revival of these practices by Scripture's own terms rather than their therapeutic rebranding.

pos: adj. (most bad; lowest in quality, character, or severity)
etymology: From Old English wyrsta, the superlative of wyrsa, worse, itself from an Indo-European root meaning to confuse or entangle; worst names the furthest extreme of a thing's badness.
biblical_def:
Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled.

Ezekiel's oracle pronounces covenant judgment on Jerusalem by threatening to hand the city over not merely to a hostile power but to the worst of the heathen, intensifying the judgment by the quality of the instrument used to execute it. The surrounding context (violence, bloodshed, idolatry filling the land) explains why the LORD selects so severe an agent: a nation that has corrupted itself past ordinary discipline receives a correspondingly severe rod. The pomp of the strong ceasing and the holy places defiled complete the reversal, since Jerusalem's own holy places had already been defiled by the idolatry the chapter has just catalogued; the judgment simply makes visible, through foreign hands, a desecration the people had already committed themselves spiritually. Worst here names deliberate severity in the instrument of judgment, not arbitrary cruelty; it is Scripture's consistent pattern that the LORD matches the severity of discipline to the depth of covenant unfaithfulness, however painful that proportion proves for the nation under judgment.

webster_full: WORSE, a. More bad or evil; inferior in quality or condition.

Ezekiel 7 insists the reverse: the severity of the worst of the heathen as the chosen instrument corresponds exactly to the severity of Jerusalem's own prior unfaithfulness, a sobering but coherent moral logic running through the LORD's governance of nations.

pos: n. (the quality of yielding no benefit; ineffectiveness toward an intended end)
etymology: From un-, not, + profit, Latin proficere, to advance or benefit, + -ableness; unprofitableness names a thing's failure to advance the end it was meant to serve.
biblical_def:
For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.

Hebrews argues at length that the Levitical priesthood and the law given through it, though holy and given by God, could never itself perfect the conscience or bring the worshiper to true completion, since it rested on repeated animal sacrifices that could never finally deal with sin and on a priesthood that died and had to be replaced generation after generation. The disannulling, the setting aside of the former commandment, is explained here by two linked words: weakness, its inherent inability to accomplish final atonement, and unprofitableness, its failure to actually advance the worshiper toward the perfection it gestured toward but could not deliver. This is not a charge that the law was sinful or worthless in its own time; Hebrews has already called it a shadow of good things to come. Unprofitableness names a limitation built into the system by design, since its whole purpose was to point forward to a better priest and a better sacrifice, Christ Himself, by whom we draw nigh unto God, as the very next verses declare. The old covenant's unprofitableness is therefore the necessary shadow proving the substance of the new.

webster_full: PROFITABLE, a. Yielding profit, gain, or advantage; useful; beneficial.

pos: n. (the state of being laid waste; desolation)
etymology: From waste, Latin vastus, empty or desolate, + -ness; wasteness names the condition of a thing emptied and ruined, applied by the prophets to land stripped bare by judgment.
biblical_def:
That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness.

Zephaniah piles up five pairs of nouns to describe the coming day of the LORD, and wasteness and desolation form the central pair, naming the land's physical and social ruin that follows divine judgment. The accumulation itself is the point: no single phrase could capture the day's severity, so the prophet stacks wrath, trouble, distress, wasteness, desolation, darkness, gloominess, clouds, and thick darkness into a single relentless description, echoing and intensifying the darkness-language of the plagues and of Sinai. Wasteness answers directly to the complacency the chapter has just indicted, those who say in their heart, the LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil; the day itself will answer that unbelief with undeniable, visible ruin. The New Testament later reuses day of the LORD language for final judgment, so Zephaniah's wasteness functions as both a historical warning to Judah and a pattern for the greater and final day still to come, in which every false security built on complacent unbelief will likewise be laid waste.

pos: adj. (full of woe; deeply sorrowful or calamitous)
etymology: From woe, an interjection of grief found across the Germanic languages, + -ful; woeful names a day or condition saturated with sorrow and calamity.
biblical_def:
As for me, I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee: neither have I desired the woeful day; thou knowest: that which came out of my lips was right before thee.

Jeremiah's confession comes in the midst of relentless persecution for faithfully delivering the LORD's hard message of coming judgment to a people who hated him for it. He protests that he has not hastened from being a pastor, that is, he did not abandon his shepherding calling to escape the cost of proclaiming it, and crucially, he has not desired the woeful day he was commanded to announce. The prophet who must speak of coming calamity is not thereby a man who delights in calamity; Jeremiah weeps over Jerusalem even as he pronounces its judgment, and this verse makes that heart explicit under direct appeal to the LORD's own knowledge, thou knowest. Woeful day names the judgment Jeremiah faithfully proclaimed at enormous personal cost precisely because faithfulness required it, not because he wished it on his own people. The verse models the proper posture of every true messenger of hard truth: faithful proclamation married to genuine grief, never satisfaction, over what that truth requires announcing.

pos: v. (past tense of yell; cried out with a loud, fierce noise)
etymology: From Old English gellan, to resound or cry loudly, related to the roots behind yell and gale; used of the fierce roaring cry of a predator over its prey.
biblical_def:
The young lions roared upon him, and yelled, and they made his land waste: his cities are burned without inhabitant.

Jeremiah pictures Israel as a scattered sheep driven away by lions, with Assyria and Babylon in view as the devouring powers whose roaring and yelling fill out the image of merciless, predatory conquest. The young lions roared upon him describes the first assault, and yelled intensifies it, the fierce cry of beasts that have already begun to tear at their prey rather than merely threaten it; the devastation named right after, land made waste and cities burned without inhabitant, shows the roaring was no empty noise. The prophets consistently use lion imagery for the terrifying, overwhelming power of pagan empires the LORD raises up as instruments of covenant judgment against His own unfaithful people, a use that in no way excuses those empires' own cruelty, which the prophets elsewhere judge in turn. Yelled captures the specific horror of judgment executed by an enemy that takes evident, fierce delight in the kill, a detail Scripture does not soften even while insisting the judgment itself was deserved and divinely permitted for Israel's own covenant unfaithfulness.

pos: n. (instances of roaming without fixed course; here, a life of fugitive distress)
etymology: From Old English wandrian, to roam or move without fixed course, + the plural noun suffix; wanderings names the repeated, often sorrowful movement of one fleeing danger or lacking settled refuge.
biblical_def:
Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?

David, fleeing for his life, likely composed during his flight from Saul, appeals to the LORD's intimate, recorded knowledge of his fugitive distress. Thou tellest my wanderings claims that every forced, fearful movement from refuge to refuge has been counted and known by God, not lost or unnoticed; put thou my tears into thy bottle extends the same claim to his sorrow itself, as though each tear were gathered and kept rather than wasted. Are they not in thy book? turns both claims into a settled confidence rather than a request, appealing to a divine record David trusts already exists. The verse answers the isolation fugitive suffering produces, the sense that no one is tracking one's scattered, frightened movements or counting one's grief, with the doctrine that the LORD Himself keeps both the wandering and the weeping in His own book. This grounds comfort not in the wanderer's own strength to endure but in the certainty of being seen, known, and recorded by God throughout every leg of an unwanted, sorrowful journey.

webster_full: WANDER, v.i. To ramble; to rove; to go without a certain course or direction.
WANDERINGS, n. Instances of roaming without fixed course; here, fugitive and sorrowful flight.

pos: adj. (worthy of trust; faithful and reliable)
etymology: From trust, likely from Old Norse traust, confidence or firmness, + -y; trusty names a person proven reliable enough to be relied upon.
biblical_def:
He removeth away the speech of the trusty, and taketh away the understanding of the aged.

Job, in the midst of his own suffering, meditates on the LORD's sovereign power to humble and dismantle human sources of confidence, naming princes, judges, kings, priests, the mighty, and counsellors all brought low by God's hand in the surrounding verses. The trusty here are those ordinarily relied upon for sound, dependable speech, the very ones a community turns to precisely because their word has proven reliable; yet even their speech can be removed by the LORD's sovereign action, just as understanding can be stripped from the aged, whose accumulated years of wisdom are no guarantee against God's power to set them aside. Job's point within his larger argument is not cynicism about human reliability as such, but a humbling reminder that every human source of dependable counsel, however proven, remains utterly subject to the LORD who gave it and can as easily take it away. The trusty man's speech is genuinely trustworthy while the LORD grants it; it is never independently, permanently secure against His sovereign hand.

corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that even the most proven, reliable human counsel remains utterly subject to God's sovereign hand and is never independently or permanently secure.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply become somewhat archaic in ordinary speech.

The humility Job's meditation presses is still needed wherever institutions or individuals place final confidence in proven experts, elders, or trusted advisors as though their reliability were self-sustaining rather than a gift continually held in God's hand. Job 12:20 does not devalue trusty counsel; it relativizes every human source of it before the LORD who can remove it at will.
